The main takeaway from our work is that

the Enterobactericeae have evolved to exploit the human host in ways that make antibiotic resistance a natural part of bacterial physiology, and the clinical implications of these evolutionary processes are profound.

the clinical and public health implications of resistance are far more complex than the mere presence or absence of a resistance gene, as the clinical outcome is determined by the interaction between host, pathogen, and environment.

the clinical management of infections caused by Enterobacteriacea will require a better understanding of the molecular epidemiology of the resistance genes that are responsible for the spread of antibiotic resistance.
